utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to deal with one preliminary, procedural matter, quickly. Yesterday the Chamber has received a filing of the Defence requesting an enlargement of an additional 14 days to respond to the Prosecution motion of the 29th of November. That was the Prosecution's motion for reconsideration of decision denying admission of 24 associated exhibits regarding RM514, or, alternatively, granting the admission of certain associated exhibits from the bar table, or certification. The current deadline for the Defence to respond to the Prosecution's motion is this week, today, Thursday, the 13th of December, and in light of the upcoming winter recess, the Chamber hereby grants the request for an extension of time. Then for the witness to enter the courtroom, we have to move into -- private session would do. It's the same as closed session here.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll take a break. We will resume ten minutes past 3.00. Is the next witness ready? And is the Prosecution ready to call him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was not sure when Your Honours would want to deal with the issue of the admissibility of the amalgamated statement, pursuant to -- or the associated exhibits pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can do it now. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, in the -- the issues have been reduced over the course of the witness's testimony. I would posit that if my understanding at this point - and Ms. Stewart will certainly correct me if I'm incorrect - is that we have three exhibits that have not -- let me say it this way. I have three exhibits that have not been objected to by the Defence that I would tender as associated exhibits, although if Your Honours would like to deal with the amalgamated statement first that may also be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the amalgamated statement, I think we -- are there any further submissions to be made, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There are not. They are contained in our written filing of the 29th of November, 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing to be added to that. The amalgamated statement which has received, I think, P628, if my recollection serves me well, is admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honours, turning to the associated exhibits. My -- by my count there are three exhibits that have not been objected to which, first, the Prosecution would tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If would you take them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. The first is 65 ter 10823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of objections, Madam Registrar, it would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours before the number is assigned, the list of documents has a number of 10832. Can counsel clarify the last two digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry it is actually 10823. 10832, I believe, was tendered under seal just shortly ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In that case the number will be Exhibit P633.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to have it under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let me just check my chart, Your Honours. Yes, this one is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P633 is admitted under seal. Next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Also no objection on 65 ter 10824. So the Prosecution would tender that under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that, Madam Registrar, would be P634, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Also no objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal, is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 65 ter 1150, the Prosecution would tender that under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there's an error. I don't see that one on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a lot of documents starting with 1150, but another number follows, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps I misread the number. It is at the top of the third page of our exhibit list which is 11510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear now. And that should be under seal? No, perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, that one is also tendered under seal. My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the specific reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you would please bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's admitted under seal. P635 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And so not addressing those documents that have already been admitted or are otherwise withdrawn, that, by our count, leaves four documents. And I would take them one at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so and could we keep in mind that if there's any confidentiality in them we should return in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honours. I will be tendering some of these under seal, so perhaps to be safe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That in itself is not a reason to move into private session but it may be better to do it. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I didn't --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was an issue regarding redactions, so perhaps I'll reserve that for my colleague to raise [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what you could -- what you could do is try to agree with Mr. Ivetic on further redactions and then inform the Chamber if there's any agreement between the parties. We will take a break, and we will resume at 20 minutes -- at 25 minutes past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the next witness, will it be you, Ms. Bolton, who will examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It will be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, since the same protective measures apply, we have to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to be requesting a document, and I would ask that it not be broadcast publicly, please, Your Honour, and that would be 65 ter 28597.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, in the document before you, do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could that be tendered, please, as the next Prosecution exhibit under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that your date of birth as it appears, is correct as well, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Until further notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 28597 will be Exhibit P639, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to respond briefly to the last words spoken in private session, no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness was in the city of Sarajevo in 1993. He observed SRK shelling of the civilian population of the city. During the first three months of the year, the average number of shells impacting the city was approximately 1200 per day. Some of the shelling was random and did not appear to have any military purpose. At times, the shelling appeared to be in retaliation for events taking place outside of Sarajevo. On the 21st of March, 1993, approximately 2400 shells were fired into Sarajevo, including 400 shells on the old town alone. The witness observed that the attack appeared to be in retaliation for an ABiH offensive launched against VRS positions on the Pale road, in an apparent attempt to sever the VRS supply lines. The witness also recalls the shelling of a football match on the 1st of June, 1993, in Dobrinja. A crater analysis determined the shells were likely fired by SRK troops at Lukavica barracks. The witness observed that civilians were targeted by VRS snipers. Civilians erected makeshift protective barriers at junctions throughout the city to protect against sniper fire. Civilians also endeavoured to flee from Sarajevo across the airport runway which was the only means of leaving or entering the city at that time, and they were also subjected to VRS sniper fire. Approximately a third of those killed or wounded at the airport were elderly persons, women, or children. The witness noticed that both shell fire and sniper fire stopped whenever cease-fires were entered into by the warring parties. The witness believed that General Galic had effective command and control over both his artillery and the snipers as a result and observed that the entire VRS structure was a strict hierarchical structure. UNPROFOR protested shelling and sniping of civilians on a number of occasions. That concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have further questions for the witness, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we move back into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, when I pose the next question to you, if you feel it's something that we need to move into private session for, would you please let me know. And my question for you, sir, is whether you could please describe the living conditions that were experienced by the civilian population in Sarajevo in middle of January 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived in Sarajevo at the (redacted) (redacted), the town was completely under siege. The local population survived thanks to the air-lifts that brought in supplies from the UNHCR and also thanks to land convoys that would reach the town. And, on the whole, they were UNHCR convoys. The town had very few energy resources because there were often power cuts, and the pumps that provide supply didn't work. The electricity was lacking, so it was obscure in the town, and you could only see some light from the heating or the lighting that used gas to function as a rule. The inhabitants tried to find water in the Manjaca river that passes through Sarajevo and, in addition to all that, what was most remarkable at the time is that there was artillery fire on a permanent basis on the town, and this has already been said. In certain cases there were military targets and there were attacks or counter-attacks launched by the various part parties. But in other cases, to my mind, the attacks were carried out in order to terrorise the population in Sarajevo. The troops who were on the front line, what I noticed is -- as I myself was in the town, what I noticed is that the Bosniak troops, the Muslim or Bosniak troops, went to the front line in the evening on the whole to relieve other troops. I saw them going to the front lines from inside the town. And, in particular, this was done at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just going to interrupt you there, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I propose to put to the witness, Your Honour, a portion of his previous evidence which had been admitted under seal. But if the documents could not be broadcast, it could be dealt with in open session, if that's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement provided in the year 2000, which is now P640, at -- and you should have that document before you, sir. You'll see that there are page numbers in the top right corner of the page written in red, and if you need to refer to the page, please, do so. It would be page 13 in all languages. And in response to the third question on that page under the heading "sniping," you stated: "I think it was important for the Serb side to exercise a permanent pressure of terror. They would do sniping therefore from a certain number of positions that we were able to determine." Just to be clear, again, who did you observe the Serb side to be attempting to terrorise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The local population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did -- did they appear to be -- VRS forces appear to be deliberately targeting civilians with sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They targeted any person moving about in the street. More specifically, at cross-roads where they could shoot down the street, which was counteracted by large sways of cloths that barred the road which gave -- on these streets, gave on to neighbourhoods where the snipers could shoot from. On the other hand, there were shelters which had been set up, made out of car or tramway carcasses. Some contingents in town guaranteed the security of the civilians who tried to move about in town on foot by using their armoured vehicles as mobile shelters to make the crossing of the town for this -- civilians easier when they were potentially in line of sight of these snipers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did the victims of this kind of sniping include any women or children or elderly persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For, among the population, there were many of these people, since most able-bodied men had been mobilised and were fighting. But I did see with my own eyes a number of bodies of elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there ever occasions or how frequently was it that people would be injured by -- or would be shot when there was no exchange of fire between the warring parties at that particular location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that what was specific to the snipers is concerned, i.e., their action against the town, these were not combat operations. These were actions aimed deliberately at the population, in order to terrorise the population and to make sure that the people would feel terrorised. People wanted to go and fetch water in the river and fetch wood, in order to be able to heat themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You just mentioned people going to fetch water and going to fetch wood. Were people targeted when they were undertaking those kinds of activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were targeted when they could be fired at from positions which would make that possible. Generally these positions or these were located on -- along the larger roads of the city. I remember the larger routes in the Grbavica neighbourhood which were occupied by the Serb forces, and these faced the large avenue running through the town. So at all the cross-roads, people who crossed these cross-roads were likely to be shot at.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On that same topic, at page 17 of the same statement in all languages, you describe the Serb forces: "Opening fire indiscriminately every night from the south-east side of the airport raking the runway with fire, as people were passing across." Could I ask you whether you had -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we move into private session for the completion of my question, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We will adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow morning, Friday, the 14th of December, at 8.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
